title.narrative: She Leads Sierra Leone

description.narrative:
Currently we are witnessing a rise in girls and young women’s activism and protest. The She Leads programme will partner with existing GYW-led groups and feminist organizations. Importantly, special efforts are made to support existing informal groups of girls and young women, for example girls clubs, associations, student groups and unregistered organizations, which have started to organize and mobilize but are often excluded from many funding mechanisms.
The programme builds directly on the experiences of the previous Girls Advocacy Alliance (2016-2020) that was also implemented in Sierra Leone
FEMNET and DCI-ECPAT are network organisations, and will be working in all countries through selected members of their respective networks. Plan International and Terre des Hommes will work through their country offices and with local contracted organisations to implement projects under the overall She Leads programme.
The is no Dutch Embassies present in Sierra Leone, but She Leads will seek support and alignment with the Dutch Embassy in Ghana where needed. Finally, She Leads will seek alignment and collaboration with other consortiums funded under the Strengthening Civil Society framework of the Dutch Ministry of Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation. In particular, She Leads will seek alignment with the four other consortiums funded under the Women’s Rights and Gender Equality (WRGE) theme of the Power of Voices funding mechanism.

Girls and young women’s (GYW’s) rights to engage in public decision-making are enshrined in international agreements and national laws. In reality, however, GYW voices are excluded from the socio-political domain, particularly those of GYW who experience intersecting forms of discrimination. GYW’s meaningful participation is obstructed by three interrelated factors. Firstly, discriminatory gender- and age-related social norms limit GYW’s rights to move freely, voice opinions and engage in public life. Secondly, GYW groups in civil society are under resourced and lack strong ties with more established CSOs. The latter are not always responsive to the specific needs and perspectives of GYW-led groups. Furthermore, the global phenomenon of shrinking civic space is affecting GYW-led organizations, making it even harder for them to express their opinions, assemble and associate. Groups that challenge the ruling gender ideology are increasingly being intimidated, threatened and exposed to violence. In conflict and humanitarian contexts, GYW actors risk additional security threats as easy targets of militarized and extremist forces. Thirdly, political institutions at local and national level are dominated by elites consisting of mainly male, elder leaders, with no interest in institutional reforms that would make decision-making processes more inclusive, transparent and accountable. Existing consultation mechanisms (such as youth parliaments and advisory bodies) are usually poorly resourced, dependent on donor support and functioning irregularly.

SUMMARY In Sierra Leone, girls and young women, particularly GYW from socially excluded and exploited groups, are denied the opportunity to voice their interests and to participate meaningfully in decision-making processes. She Leads is a joint programme of Plan International Netherlands, Defence for Children - ECPAT the Netherlands (DCI-ECPAT), African Women’s Development and Communication Network (FEMNET), and Terre des Hommes the Netherlands (TdH). Equal Measures 2030 is a technical partner. In Sierra Leone, She Leads members Plan International , Defence for Children and Femnet. They will bring together child rights organisations, feminist/women’s rights organisations, and GYW-led groups with the aim to increase sustained influence of girls and young women (GYW) on decision-making and the transformation of gender norms in formal and informal institutions. The programme will be implemented in Bo, Bombali, Kenema, Koinadugu, Moyamba, Tonkalili and Western Area.

She Leads contributes to a lasting transformative effect on engagement of GYW in decision-making. The following strategies will be implemented:
1. Strengthening and resourcing GYW-led organizations: investing in the resource base of GYW-led organizations will help them access other funding in the future. 2. Support social movements: social movements can accelerate lasting change in societies’ structures and norms. She Leads will bring together child-rights and feminist organisations and GYW-led groups to push collectively for transformative change in gender norms, and for institutional reform. 3. Engaging boys & men, parents, and traditional and religious leaders: these actors are crucial allies to ensure structural change and permanent effects when it comes to norms change. Because of their status and their role in socialisation processes, these actors promote structural change in societies. 4. Engaging media: She Leads will use media as a tool to amplify GYWs voices, and will target media as a powerful agent of change. Opening space for GYW’s voices and leadership in the media will ultimately influence broader communities, and has lasting effects beyond the programme. 5. Organisational capacity strengthening of CSO’s: investments in advocacy capacity, building relationships with decision-makers, strengthening fundraising skills will have a lasting effect on their influencing work beyond She Leads. 6. Linking local, national, regional and global: She Leads is implemented at different levels that are strategically interconnected. Interventions and results in one domain trigger change in other domains, and changes at local, national, regional and international levels are connected and influence each other.

She Leads envisions change in 3 domains of society: the social-cultural, civil society and institutional domain. In the social-cultural domain, partners engage traditional and religious leaders, forging coalitions of progressive actors who, due to their status and authority, will galvanize their constituencies to adopt more positive gender and age norms. Awareness raising and diffusion of new ideas through media and peer networks (including boys and young men) will challenge existing norms and expectations. Young female activists play an important role in this process, by inspiring other girls and breaking down negative stereotypes. In the civil society domain, the creation (consolidation) of safe spaces in which GYW can meet, exchange, build their confidence, political consciousness and skills, is a major step towards increased self-organization. Another key condition is the increased capacity of (adult-led) CSOs to effectively support GYW collective action. Stronger collaboration between GYW groups, child and women’s rights networks will lead to a more enabling environment for GYW-led groups. A well connected and better resourced social movement for girls’ rights is able to promote a strong feminist counternarrative to the dominant patriarchal and ageist ideology. In the institutional domain, policy makers will develop greater awareness and knowledge about GYW inclusion in decision-making. Stronger connections between progressive policy makers and political leaders working at different levels will result in a coalition of reform-minded champions. In addition, pressure exercised by regional and international bodies will force national governments to take action and safeguard GYW’s rights to association and freedom of expression.

To facilitate the change process towards the She Leads’ strategic objective, consortium members and partners have opted to implement the following mix of strategies and actions:
• support girls and young women led groups, to be able to champion advocacy issues and also enhance their skills, to participate in decision making in CSO platforms. Support will include trainings in facilitating advocacy, communication, leadership, proposal writing and management skills. They will also provided with funds after been capacitated to carry out their advocacy.
• support to the CSO partners to be able to mentor girls and young women’s groups to carry out their activism. This support will include assessment, capacity building by the consortium partners and country partners to CSOs. In addition, CSO partners will link girls and young women’s group with existing networks, coalitions and forums. This will help to increase the chances of GYW to participate in decision making process and also advocacy at national and international level.
• organize quarterly learning sessions of GYW to create learning opportunities for girls and young women’s group, as well as to identify the successes and challenges that the groups are faced with whilst carrying out their initiatives.
• engage Child Right and Gender sensitive CSO’s and non-governmental organizations: Civil society organisations that promote gender and child rights, will be targeted during the implementation. They will lobby to provide additional support (technical and financial) to girls and young women’s group, and also identify further funding opportunities for them as well. This will help to increase the capacity (financial and technical) of GYW groups to influence decision making bodies on their participation.
• facilitating media advocacy for girls and young women’ group: Girls and young women will be capacitated through training on media advocacy and also provided with necessary equipment including video cameras and digital cameras that will enhance their advocacy to themedia, including social and traditional media. This strategy will help to amplify their voices and help widen their advocacy platforms.
• Intergenerational dialogues with community stakeholders, on discriminatory social and gender norms excluding GYW from decision-making. The essence of these dialogues is to understand the negative norms and practices affecting women’s empowerment, and also their participation in decision making process. n.
• mobilizing community champions/role models, men, boys, parents to challenge negative social and gender norms. Support will be provided to community champions to organize events that will inspire community members to change their negative norms and practices. Also, community leaders will be influenced to publicly challenge and condemn the negative norms and practices existing in their communities. In addition, changing negative norms required a lot of practical sessions with stakeholders that are involved.
• sessions on gender socialization, living in peace and life skills will be organized. These will involve girls and young women, boys and young men, at community level. These are practical sessions that will help men and women to understand gender roles, how to support each other whilst carrying out their gender roles, and most important, the importance of promoting gender equality.
• dialogue with GYW on the effects of negative social and gender norms limiting their participation in decision making: Girls and young women will be engage in dialogue sessions, that will help them acquire skills, to challenge their perceived gender role. This venture will help to increase their representation in male dominated areas. In addition, under this strategy, schools will be provided with support to build the confidence and skills of girls and young women, to aspire for school leadership positions.
• provide input to the government to review existing laws and policies and also develop new ones that promote girls and young women’s empowerment. The Ministry of social Welfare will be supported to review the Child Right Act, Child Marriage Laws, and also develop the Gender Equality policy. The Ministry of Youth will be supported to implement the Youth Policy.
• engage Ministries, and institutions to support the involvement of girls and young women in leadership and decision-making process.
• identify champions who will create the space for girls and young women, within their institutions.
• engage the Commission for political party registration. This commission is responsible for harmonizing and coordinating the affairs of political parties. Hence engaging them to create space for girls and young women’s participation, will contribute to bringing the issues of girls and young women in the agenda of political parties.

Within the population of girls and young women (between 14 till 24 years), the programme aims to strengthen the influence and participation of GYW who suffer most from (intersectional) discrimination and exclusion. These include: • GYW living in poor, remote rural areas and urban slums • GYW experiencing gender based violence (particularly girls who have married early) • GYW with disabilities • GYW who are out of school • Refugee and internally displaced GYW • GYW from sexual minority groups

title.narrative: # of CSOs (not youth or women led) that have enhanced representation of constituencies.

comment.narrative: At the start of the programme, the baseline value for this indicator is 0

Plan International Sierra Leone has made great strides in strengthening its representational role towards girls and young women. It restructured its Youth Advisory Panel to ensure a more equal representation and participation from young people from a broader range of districts of Sierra Leone. The YAP now has 61 members (38 girls and young women, 23 boys and young men). The YAP members are also having regular meetings with the country leadership team members.
Plan International Sierra Leone continue to strengthen its representational role towards girls and young women.

Plan International Sierra Leone, alongside the overall country She Leads network, has influenced the Ministry of Gender to consider participation of Girls and Young led groups in their quarterly meetings for their ideas on girls' rights and gender equality. This is based on their participation in the district and national coordination meetings of key ministries and Departments such as Ministry of Gender and Children’s Affairs, Ministry of Social Welfare, Youth Commission, Ministry of Education, District Council, movements and networks within the districts.

Plan International Sierra Leone succesfully supported 12 women from the Koinadugu Women's Network who gained representation at the National Young Women Governance Network Sierra Leone. The National Young Women Network is a body that is formed for all women that are advocates for the rights and empowerment of the girl child in Sierra Leone. The 12 women that gained the representation at the Northern Region are involved in all decision-making processes.
The new partners will expand their outreach to groups of girls and young women, engaging them more actively in project activities.

title.narrative: # youth led of CSOs that have enhanced representation of constituencies.

comment.narrative: At the start of the programme, the baseline value for this indicator is 0
These youth-led CSOs are succesfully mobilizing boys and young men to become champions for gender equality

The main target of this indicator is CFN. During 2023, this partner was able to strengthen its influencing interventions on girls' rights issues, in particular girls' rights to participation. CFN influenced positive parenting and contributed to a shift in attitudes towards raising the girl child among communities in Western Area. Parents are now much more supportive of their girls and young women to voice out their challenges and participate in various community development engagements. Stakeholders such as chiefs, mammy queens, parents, boys and young men, religious leaders, heads of community structures and social groups show increased levels of commitment to support GYW and giving them leadership space. A key example is the increase in girls and young women who are being elected as class representatives at their school.

title.narrative: # women led of CSOs that have enhanced representation of constituencies.

comment.narrative: At the start of the programme, the baseline value for this indicator is 0
CARL and ADPSL have included physically challenged GYW into their programs

ADPSL has managed to strengthen its interventions implemented with and for girls and young women. Through its influence on local cultural decision-making courts, it has achieved to open these spaces for more girls and young women's participation. For example, the Sherbro Tribal Chief in Tombo community, Western Rural Area, in a stakeholders meeting in the community extended invitation to the GYW group in the community to send two representatives who for the first time were part of the council of Sherbro local court. The representative is to attend all sittings of the court. Additionally, for the first time, the Chief in Dwarzack community during a meeting held with the community granted membership space to two GYW to be part of the community council of elders and local court committee where they would attend meetings and witness case hearings in the community local court.
This refers to the capacity of CARL and ADPSL to integrate GYW voices in their organizations

Although CARL and ADPSL have gained more organizational strength through the implementation of She Leads activities aimed at the meaningful inclusion and participation of GYW, the effects in terms of their representational capacity still need to materialize.

GYW led groups were identified and assessed to know their capacity and strength to develop and implement activities on their own. Total of 20 groups have been assessed and training and coaching support started. Results are expected during next year.

Support management in strengthening the relationship-building skills of their staff and facilitating their access to relevant coordination platforms have strengthened SLADA's representational role. SLADA has empowered their field staff on how to engage in activism and policy advocacy by providing the platforms to attend donor and coordination meetings. SLADA has a bigger network as they are implementing for CARE, Purposeful and other Plan Projects. They maintain a good working relationship with government line ministries.The organization is headed by a young woman woman, the Head of Program is a young woman and they are operating in 3 districts (Western Area ,Moyamba, Port Loko and Pujehun).

In 2021, Plan International Sierra Leone reported an increase in its capacity to work with and engage GYW-led groups. During 2022, the capacity was further consolidated. This has been demonstrated in the successful implementation of the youth resourcing pilot and the facilitation of GYW representatives in national and international policy dialogues.

title.narrative: # of CSOs which are both women and youth led with strengthened capacity to advance women’s rights and gender equality

comment.narrative: At the start of the programme, the value for this indicator is 0
2 GYW-led groups whose capacity to advocate and connect to key decision-makers will be strengthened
The GYW-led groups identified in the target are the Tier 3 partners of Plan International. The support provided to them during 2023 is included in our narrative annual report.
These are 8 GYW led groups working on the She Leads project; 4 in Moyamba, 2 in Koinadugu and 4 in Western Area

Three GYW-led organizations successfully applied for She Leads funding. They have also been trained and coached by Plan International Sierra Leone on three specific topics: the collection of evidence supporting their advocacy claims, the use of this evidence in regional and international advocacy opportunities and the organization of a GYW-led summit to facilitate the connections between different GYW-led groups

No tier 2 partners in this category. But ongoing capacity support to the informal GYW-led groups and networks which are supported. Two GYW led groups ( She Empowerment League and Youth Initiave Action for Climate Change ) were provided with capacity trainings by involving them in trainings that will be conducted for contracted CSO. The 2 youth groups that were supported technically and financially have gained strength and capacity in implementing gender equality and children's rights activities through the coaching and mentoring, and their involvement in trainings and workshops organized by the project. YICA has able to get an office space and a well structured staffing. Additionally, Youth Initiative for Climate Action (YICA): launched the first local chapter of the Youth Climate Council Freetown, which is currently operating under the Mayor's Office and various ministries focused on climate change in Freetown. They also gained funding from the Global Human Rights to implement a one-year-long mentoring climate action program for 20 women in Sierra Leone and also provided funding for 5 Girls and Young Women to lead climate action The She Empowerment League was also contracted by GIZ to provide a one week training for their staff on Gender related issues.
The three new (tier 3) groups will receive capacity support in project management, resource mobilization and lobby and advocacy strategies.
